title: "Gamified" learning apps stink... how do you build actually fun educational games while not fully abandoning the education aspect
author: potateo2
selftext:
There seems to be a big tradeoff between a game that is fun or something that is educational. When building something educational, you hope the player's desire to learn makes up for the fact that the game is not as fun as something else they could be playing.

Anyone building cool in-game features that would close this gap? Are there titles out there that close this gap well? I want to build some personal finance educational game but am having trouble figuring out this dilemma.   
  
In my mind, Oregon Trail is the gold standard because the learning went hand in hand with the game. Super open to discussion on how the learning experience can change with ai in gaming

comments.author: ffxivthrowaway03
comments.body: Why are you acting under the false assumption that learning and fun are mutually exclusive?

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
*Literally* their second sentence, emphasis mine:

>When building something educational, you hope the player's desire to learn **makes up for the fact that the game is not as fun** as something else they could be playing.

That is a direct claim that as a game's educational value increases, fun decreases.

replies.author: potateo2
replies.body:
Maybe a better expression of my idea would be zero sum, not mutually exclusive. 

I guess my point is that it is very common for games to live closer to a side of the spectrum, rather than clearly offer fun and educational value equally. 

Building games that sit around that fulcrum I think can harder, and maybe that’s why there’s seemingly less?

replies.author: No-Marionberry-772
replies.body:
its a very real and common trend. its also not them stating that education and fun are mutually exclusive. 

its stating that in most typical cases, educational value comes at a cost of fun game design, and its a largely true statement.  

education itself can be fun to a person who is interested in the specific subject matter and is fascinated by it, but that is not a game, that is education, and its not what they are talking 
 about.

the entire premise of the post is looking for games where the trade off is minimized or eliminated.

replies.author: ffxivthrowaway03
replies.body:
You're making an *assumption* of what they meant that runs contrary to the words on the page.

>education itself can be fun to a person who is interested in the specific subject matter and is fascinated by it, but that is not a game, that is education, and its not what they are talking   about.

You are literally making the same erroneous logical jump that OP is - education and "what is a game" are not mutually exclusive things. Games can be educational, and education can be a game, and one is not *inherently* at odds with the other.  Is it harder to design a game that doesn't feel like attending a lecture if your goal is to educate?  Yes.  Can you sit here and go "education cannot be a game, it's education!"  Absolutely not, and OP's own list of games that do exactly that is directly contradictory to that notion.

But whatever, downvote and move on.

comments.author: AverageDrafter
comments.body:
Civilization - Absorbing the tech tree from Civ 1 gave me a roadmap to later explore world history and made connections I didn't understand at the time, but learned by they were that way in the game - like Communism requiring Industrialization as a prereq.  Its a game concept that translates to how it happened, but isn't an obvious "learn this" lesson.

Music Theory requires Mathmatics.  Then you learn a bit about music theory and understand why.

replies.author: potateo2
replies.body:
So this is kinda exactly it. Games can exhibit very real educational value, that you managed to extract. But for most, the reason for playing Civ 1 is not to learn about communism or history, it’s the fun behind building the civilization and the rest comes with. 

For someone who’s like I want to learn finance, math, or something of the sort, there has to be some sort of game that can achieve that while still being fun. Or better than something that just asks multiple choice questions and slaps a steak counter on there to call it gamified

replies.author: silly_bet_3454
replies.body:
Take a game like factorio, it's a very fun way to learn some engineering practices because that's the actual theme and goal of the game. So you can apply that idea to anything.

You want to learn finance, take a game like lemonade tycoon, it's all about making business decisions. You could expand on that idea and add things like debt and credit and leverage and so on but it all goes towards this goal of taking calculate risks and decisions to make your business succeed.

I can't think of a great one off top of mind for math, but think about what do people try to do with math in the real world. It's more abstract. If it's just basic arithmetic you could have a game like where you're a cashier and you have to ring people up really fast and calculate change and coin breakdown for instance, that's just fun mental math training, it would play kind of like root beer tapper, that's just one example.

comments.author: Reinfeldx
comments.body: It may or may not apply here, but technology in the classroom has been found to produce worse learning outcomes, generally speaking. I know that's a slightly different topic but I guess I'd question how much traditional learning can be done with a game in the first place. No question though that games can teach *something* and can be especially good at developing some skills.

comments.author: silly_bet_3454
comments.body:
I think a lot of it has to do with simply what are your design goals for your game. When you think about duolingo, I wouldn't even call it a game, it's a learning app. I can see how there are reward mechanisms but clearly the focus is 99% around trying to master a very specific skill in a very specific format. Oregon Trail is so obviously different from that on its face, it's a game first and foremost, and the stuff you learn is secondary, it's like part of the lore and just the content of the game.

So, Idk how exactly to answer your particular question, if your goal is actually to make a game that ends up in a classroom, you're certainly going to be more limited in what you can do and you do have to prioritize a learning curriculum, that makes it very hard to also make a fun game. Still though, you can make "fun" a top priority from your design perspective, start by just trying to come up with fun mechanics, and then layer in whatever content you care about secondarily. Obviously something like Duolingo or Khan Academy makes zero effort to put any kind of actual mechanics in their game.

comments.author: DeProgrammer99
comments.body:
The information density has to be somewhat sparse to make room for the fun parts. Games generally center around a gameplay loop--something you do over and over, and if you get good enough at the game and the game is good enough, you can reach a flow state... But you can't really do that if you're constantly learning new information, because you really can't *get good at* recalling information you've just learned and haven't used before.

Most games that increase in complexity over time only add one new mechanic every 1\~10 levels, but in education, you might learn part of a concept from one sentence, three facts the next sentence, and the rest of the information wrapping up all of that nicely into a single spark of understanding with the sentence after that. And then you can't recall it from rote memory by the time you get to the end of the next page, because our brains are built to forget more information than they retain.

Also, constantly *failing* to recall facts over and over (which, again, is normal!) is mentally exhausting. It's literally how I put myself to sleep every night...with Japanese vocabulary flash cards.

So if recall is so hard and exhausting, for a game, you'd naturally want to make it easier by focusing on recognition instead of recall, like with multiple-choice questions... but that also reduces the impact on learning. It's most effective when you practice in the same way you want to perform: if you want to be able to think of a word, the most helpful learning method is to *try to think of* the word. Recognizing a written word and thinking of the definition is a decent way to learn to recognize it when spoken, but hearing it works even better. [Here's a random study since I haven't been citing sources.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC6990689/)
